chapter.title: Placing your first order

cards.body: The safest way to buy your first share is an order that might buy nothing at all. In the bazaar, placing an order means handing the shopkeeper a note. One note says *I'll pay whatever you're asking*. The other says **I'll pay ₹1,600, not a paisa more**.
cards.simpler: The safest way to buy your first share is an order that might buy nothing at all. Picture a busy bazaar. Placing an order there is like handing the shopkeeper a note. One note says *I'll pay whatever you're asking*. The other says **I'll pay ₹1,600, not a paisa more**. If the shopkeeper won't take that price, you simply walk away with your money.

cards.prompt: The board shows ₹1,612 for a share you want. You hand the stall a note: "Buy 1 at ₹1,600 or less." The price sits at ₹1,612 all afternoon. What happens?

options.text: You get the share at ₹1,612 anyway.
Nothing gets bought, and none of your money is spent.
The broker buys it at ₹1,600 and the shop takes the ₹12 hit.

whyNot.a: That's the 'whatever you're asking' note, not yours. You capped the price at ₹1,600.
whyNot.c: That's haggling, not the market. A trade only happens if a seller actually agrees to ₹1,600.

cards.reteach: Your note sets a ceiling. A trade happens only when a seller agrees to your price or lower. If no seller comes down to ₹1,600, your note just waits.

cards.title: Two notes: market and limit
cards.body:
A *market order* says: buy now, at the best price any seller is asking. It almost always *fills*, which means the trade actually happens, and it happens within a second. For a busy Nifty 50 share on a calm day, you usually pay within a few paise of the board. **You're sure to buy, but not sure of the price.**

A *limit order* works the other way round. You name the most you'll pay, and your order waits in the exchange's queue like a slip stuck on a spike at the counter.
cards.simpler: A *market order* buys now, at the best price on offer. It almost always *fills* (the trade happens) within a second. On a busy Nifty 50 share you pay within a few paise of the shown price. **You're sure to buy, but not sure of the price.** A *limit order* names your top price and waits in line, like a slip stuck on a spike at the counter.

cards.title: While your limit order waits
cards.body:
Your slip on the spike fills only if a seller meets your price or goes lower. While it waits, your broker usually sets that cash aside so you can't spend it twice.

If nobody meets your price by 3:30 pm, a normal day order is cancelled and the cash is freed. **Nothing was spent.**
cards.simpler: A limit order fills only if a seller meets your price or lower. While it waits, the cash for it is usually set aside. If nobody meets your price by 3:30 pm, it's cancelled and the cash is freed. **Nothing was spent.**

cards.title: Riya's first order
cards.body: Riya, 24, opens her broker app at 11 am on a Tuesday. The bank share she wants shows ₹1,612.40. She picks Limit, types quantity 1 (checking twice that it isn't 10) and sets her price at ₹1,605. At 1:47 pm a seller agrees to ₹1,605, and her order status flips to Executed. She saved ₹7.40, about half a cutting chai, which she drinks anyway to celebrate.
cards.simpler: Riya, 24, opens her broker app at 11 am on a Tuesday. The bank share she wants shows ₹1,612.40. She picks Limit and types quantity 1, checking twice that it isn't 10. She sets her price at ₹1,605. At 1:47 pm a seller agrees, and **her order status changes to Executed**. She saved ₹7.40, about half a cutting chai. She drinks one anyway to celebrate.

cards.prompt: Kabir wants 1 share showing ₹1,940. He will not pay more than ₹1,950, full stop. Which order matches what he wants?

whyNot.a: That's the 'whatever you're asking' note. A market order buys at the going price and has no ₹1,950 ceiling.
whyNot.c: That's the quantity and price boxes swapped. It asks for 1,950 shares at ₹1 each, and that will never buy him anything.

cards.reteach: When you have a hard top price, a limit order is how you write it down. Quantity is how many shares you want. Price is the most you'll pay for each one.

cards.title: After the tap: T+1
cards.body: Your order filled, but the share isn't in your demat locker yet. India settles most trades on *T+1*: the trade day plus one working day. **Buy on Friday, and it lands in your demat on Monday**, unless Monday is a market holiday. The taxes and fees on the way in get their own chapter later.
cards.simpler: Your order filled, but the share isn't in your demat account yet. India settles most trades on *T+1*: trade day plus one working day. **Buy on Friday, and it arrives Monday**, unless Monday is a holiday. Taxes and fees get their own chapter later.

cards.body: Dev sets a limit order at ₹1,500 while the share sits at ₹1,612. Then he closes the app and tells his flatmate he's a shareholder now. The price never drops that far, so at 3:30 pm the order quietly cancels. He finds out on Thursday, staring at an empty demat. How to spot it: open the Orders tab and check that the status says **Executed or Complete, not Open or Pending**.
cards.simpler: Dev sets a limit order at ₹1,500 while the share sits at ₹1,612. He closes the app and tells his flatmate he owns shares now. The price never drops that low, so at 3:30 pm the order quietly cancels. On Thursday he finds his demat account empty. To avoid this, open the Orders tab and check that the status says **Executed or Complete, not Open or Pending**.

cards.prompt: Your cousin says: "A limit order is just a slow market order. It always buys in the end." What's the honest reply?

options.text: True. It waits in line, but it always fills by 3:30 pm.
Not quite. It only trades if a seller meets your price. Otherwise it can cancel with nothing bought.
Backwards. The limit order is the fast one, and the market order waits for your price.

whyNot.a: That's mixing up waiting with filling. A day order that no seller meets gets cancelled at the close.
whyNot.c: That's the two notes swapped. The market order is the fast one, and it has no price limit.

cards.reteach: Picture the two notes again. 'Whatever you're asking' trades now, at any price. 'Not a paisa more than ₹1,600' trades only at that price or lower, and it may never trade at all.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A market order buys right now at whatever sellers are asking. A limit order names your top price and buys only if someone meets it, or not at all. Once it fills, the share usually reaches your demat the next working day.

Tomorrow: why a ₹3,000 share can be cheaper than a ₹50 one.
cards.simpler: A market order buys right now at whatever sellers are asking. A limit order names your top price and buys only if someone meets it, **or not at all**. Once it fills, the share usually reaches your demat account the next working day. Tomorrow: why a ₹3,000 share can be cheaper than a ₹50 one.

cards.body: Open your broker app, pick any Nifty 50 share and tap Buy. Switch between Market and Limit and notice which one adds a price box. Then back out without confirming.
cards.simpler: Open your broker app, pick any Nifty 50 share and tap Buy. Switch between Market and Limit, and **notice which one adds a price box**. That box is where your top price goes, like the note you hand the shopkeeper. Then back out without confirming, so nothing gets bought.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now buy 1 share with a limit order and say when it lands in your demat.
